chain.g: The first letter of the Latin alphabet, written in the Latin script.

ety.text: The letter name is from Middle English ā, from Old French, ultimately from Latin ā. Use of the Latin letter in (Old) English displaced the futhorc letter ᚪ (a) beginning in the 7th century, and partially also ᚫ (æ).

From Middle English a, an, from Old English ān (“one; a; lone; sole”). More at one. The "n" was gradually lost before consonants in almost all dialects by the 15th century. Cognate with Alemannic German a (“a, an”), East Franconian a (“a, an”).
* From Middle English a, o, from Old English a-, an, on. * Unstressed form of on.
From Middle English a, ha contraction of have, or haven.
From Middle English a, a reduced form of he (“he”)/ha (“he”), heo (“she”)/ha (“she”), ha (“it”), and hie, hie (“they”).
From Middle English of, with apocope of the final f and vowel reduction.
From Northern Middle English aw, alteration of all.
From the common method of counting semiquavers as "one-e-and-a, two-e-and-a" and so on.

ex: But with some prelude of disparagement, / Read, mouthing out his hollow oes and aes, / Deep-chested music, and to this result.

senses.d: An unspecified example of (something); the indefinite article.
ex: There was a man here looking for you yesterday.
Hoots the Owl: Yes a, fruit, is a , any, time, food!

senses.d: One; used before score, dozen, hundred, thousand, million, etc.
ex: I've seen it happen a hundred times.
Everybody drinks a lot in wartime, but it seemed to me that I must have drunk enough to float a couple of battleships.

senses.d: Used in some phrases denoting quantity, such as a few, a good many, a couple, a little, a bit, etc.
ex: He's a bit thick, isn't he?
They asked me a few questions.

senses.d: Used before a numeral.
ex: There are a few hundred orders that need to be fulfilled by tomorrow.
That was on the first day's walk. It took him until day three, after a good ten miles, to ask her out.

senses.d: Used in some adverbial phrases denoting the degree or extent of an action, such as a little, a bit, a lot, etc.
ex: The door was opened a little.
The bridge was shifted a bit to the east and rebuilt, this time with the shops of money-changers along both sides.

senses.d: The same; one and the same. Used in phrases such as of a kind, birds of a feather, etc.
ex: We are of a mind on matters of morals.
They're two of a kind.

senses.d: Any; every; used before a noun which has become modified to limit its scope.
ex: A man who dies intestate leaves his children troubles and difficulties.

senses.d: Any; used with a negative to indicate not a single one.
ex: It was so dark that we couldn't see a thing.
He fell all that way, and hasn't a bump on his head?

senses.d: Used before an adjective that modifies a noun (singular or plural) delimited by a numeral.
ex: The lottery jackpot is worth a staggering three hundred million dollars.
The holidays are a mere one week away.

senses.d: One; someone named; used before a person's name, suggesting that the speaker knows little about the person other than the name.
ex: We've received an interesting letter from a Mrs. Miggins of London.

senses.d: To do with separation; In, into.
ex: torn a pieces

senses.d: To do with time; Each, per, in, on, by. Often occurs between two nouns, where the first noun occurs at the end of a verbal phrase.
ex: I brush my teeth twice a day.

senses.d: To do with status; In.

senses.d: To do with position or direction; In, on, at, by, towards, onto.
ex: stand a tiptoe

senses.d: To do with process, with a passive verb; In the course of, experiencing.
ex: The times, they are a-changin'.

senses.d: To do with an action, an active verb; Engaged in.

senses.d: To do with an action/movement; To, into.

ex: He've a got a great venture on hand, but what a [it] be he tell'th no man.
